e.t: This word refers to a tamarisk, a tree or shrub known for growing in dry regions. It is a noun naming a particular kind of plant, rather than expressing an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 17:6. The word itself identifies the plant; the surrounding verse is needed to understand why it is mentioned there and what significance the passage gives it.

This word means “unleavened,” describing food made without leaven, and it can also refer to the “Feast of Unleavened Bread.” As an adjective, it identifies something prepared or observed without leaven. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 50 times, especially in passages concerning Israel’s appointed feasts and offerings. Its meaning therefore points both to the absence of leaven and, by extension, to the sacred feast associated with unleavened bread.

This Greek LXX noun means a doorpost—the upright part of a doorway to which a door is attached. It names a physical architectural feature rather than an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Ezekiel, at Ezekiel 40:48 and 41:3. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: a structural post forming or supporting the side of an entrance. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the particular doorway or building being described in either verse.

Akim is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Micah 1:10. The name itself does not provide further information about the person’s character, role, or significance; those details would come from the surrounding passage, not from the name’s basic meaning. Its lexical meaning is simply “Akim.”

Amoria is a proper name, appearing as “Amoria” in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as an ordinary descriptive word, action, or quality, but as a specific name preserved in the biblical text. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Chronicles 3:1. Without the surrounding verse text, the available information identifies the name and its location but does not establish further details about the person, place, or referent it names.

This adjective describes someone who does not perceive clearly or who lacks understanding—an “imperceptive” or “unintelligent” person. It points to a failure to grasp what should be recognized, rather than merely describing a lack of information. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 10 times across Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This adjective describes someone or something engaged in opposition—“wrestling against” another. It presents conflict as an active struggle rather than simple disagreement, portraying the opposing party as one who contends directly. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, the word occurs twice, both in deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but its central idea remains direct resistance or contest.

This Greek LXX noun means “report”—information communicated from one person to another. It refers to something told or made known, rather than to the act of speaking itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ruth 2:11, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains a report: conveyed information that enables someone to learn about an event, action, or circumstance.

This word means a “gift” or “offering”—something presented or given. It is a noun describing what is offered, rather than the act of giving. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs five times, all in Numbers 8, where its repeated use keeps the focus on something dedicated or presented. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a gift or offering given for a stated purpose.

This verb means “testify”: to give testimony or speak as a witness concerning something. It describes the action of bearing witness about a matter. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 12:30. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the exact subject and force of that testimony must be determined from the passage itself. The word’s basic meaning remains the act of giving testimony.

This verb means to make something narrow, restricted, or blocked up—to “straiten” or “block up.” It describes an action that limits passage, space, or movement rather than simply naming a condition. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, in Esther 5:1. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic idea is restriction or obstruction.

This Greek LXX verb means “smear”: to spread a substance across a surface. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament tradition represented here, in Sirach 22:1. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its precise force in that passage cannot be stated beyond this basic action. Its central meaning remains the act of applying or spreading something over another surface.

Archad, also rendered “Arkhath,” is a proper name in the Greek LXX. It identifies a named person, place, or group in the biblical text, but the available word-level information does not establish which kind of name it is. This name occurs once in the LXX, at Genesis 10:10. Its precise significance there must be understood from the verse and its surrounding passage rather than from the name alone.

This noun means “ruling jailer,” referring to the person in charge of a prison or its prisoners. It describes an authority figure responsible for overseeing the jail and managing those held there. In the Greek Old Testament, the word occurs three times, all in Genesis 39:21–23, in connection with Joseph’s imprisonment. The word’s basic sense identifies the jail’s chief keeper; the precise role it carries in any sentence depends on the surrounding passage.

This proper noun refers to Assyria or to an Assyrian person or people. It is a name rather than a general description, identifying a place, nation, or people associated with Assyria. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 124 times, especially in 2 Kings and Isaiah. Its exact reference—whether to the land, its people, or something belonging to them—depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX noun means “walk,” referring to walking or a walk as an action or activity. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, both occurrences appearing in Ezra 7:22. The word’s basic sense is therefore straightforward: it names the act of walking rather than describing a person, place, or quality. Its precise significance in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Baithagla, also rendered Vethagla, is a proper name for a place. It does not describe an action, quality, or spiritual idea; it identifies a location by name. In the Greek Septuagint text, this name occurs twice, both times in Joshua: Joshua 15:6 and Joshua 18:19. Since the available information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, its precise geographical role cannot be explained further here.

Balmainan, also given as Valmenan, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named location or person in the Greek Old Testament tradition; the available lexical information does not establish which kind without the surrounding verse text. This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at Joshua 15:24, and its precise reference is best understood from that passage’s wider list and context.

This word is a proper name identifying Barak, also rendered Varak. It functions as a person’s name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 15 times, appearing mainly in Judges and once in 1 Samuel. Its basic meaning is therefore the name Barak; the surrounding passage is needed to explain what is being said about him in any particular verse.

Βηλα is a proper name rendered “Bēla” or “Vila.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Numbers 34:11. The available wording supports understanding it as a personal name, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain which individual is meant or what role that person has in the passage.

This word means “book”: a written work or document. It is a noun used for a book as a recognizable written record, whether referring to a particular volume or to written contents. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical corpus, it occurs 17 times, showing that this is a recurring term for written material across that collection. Its precise reference in any verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the central idea remains a book or written record.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “dung” or “filth”—waste matter regarded as dirty, defiling, or worthless. It names a physical substance rather than an action or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Ezekiel and Zephaniah, and once in Sirach. Its basic sense remains direct and concrete: material treated as refuse or impurity. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself carries no broader meaning beyond this picture of dung or filth.

Garizin is a proper name, rendered “Garizin,” rather than a word describing an ordinary quality, action, or object. It identifies a specific place or named entity in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. The name occurs six times in this LXX corpus, in Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic function is identification by name rather than description.

Gērsōm, also given as Yirsom, is a proper name identifying a person in the Old Testament Greek text. It does not function as a general description or action word, but as an individual’s name. This name occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament corpus, once in 1 Chronicles 2:47 and once in Ezra 8:2. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself establishes identity but does not provide further information about the person’s role or significance.

This word means “vulture,” a large bird associated with feeding on dead animals and with soaring in the sky. It is a noun naming the bird itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, and Job. The word is used both in lists of birds and in observations about the natural world, but its basic meaning remains the same: a vulture. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “beat” or “skin.” It describes an action done to something or someone: striking, or removing skin. As a verb, it expresses an act rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament corpus, at 2 Chronicles 29:34. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic range is limited to beating or skinning.

διαγλύφω describes the action of “carve in intaglio,” making an engraved design by cutting into a material. It is a verb, so it presents this work as something being done rather than naming the finished object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Exodus, 2 Chronicles, and Ezekiel. Its references concern crafted or carved features, while the precise detail in each passage belongs to the surrounding verse context.

gl: divide and marshal; muster in array
d: divide and marshal; muster in array

e.t: This verb describes arranging things into an ordered formation: to “divide and marshal” or “muster in array.” It points to deliberate organization, especially placing people or things in their proper order rather than leaving them scattered. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 3:25. Its central meaning is clear, while its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX verb means “arrange in order”: to put things into an ordered or organized arrangement. It describes an action rather than a person or object. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 2 Maccabees 7:22. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic sense is the deliberate ordering or setting of things in a proper sequence.

This LXX adjective describes something as transcendent or differing. It can point to what surpasses or stands above others, or to what is distinct rather than the same. Its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears, but its central idea is distinction—either through superiority or difference. It occurs seven times in the LXX corpus, in passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees.

gl: cake made with oil and honey
d: cake made with oil and honey

e.h: A Cake Made with Oil and Honey
e.t: This noun means a cake made with oil and honey. It names a prepared food, rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Exodus 16:31 and Numbers 11:8, both within descriptions of food associated with Israel’s wilderness experience. The word therefore refers specifically to this kind of sweet, oil-based cake. Its exact significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

Eglam is a proper name, used to identify a specific named entity rather than express a general idea, action, or quality. Its meaning is therefore its identity as “Eglam,” not a descriptive definition such as a virtue, object, or event. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 6:54. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular referent cannot be described more specifically, but the word functions as a name in that passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to hold an assembly and debate within it. It describes gathering people together for a public meeting in which matters are discussed. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Esther. Its emphasis is not merely on people being present, but on convening them for shared discussion or deliberation. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the purpose of the gathering.

This adjective describes something made of olive wood. It identifies the material associated with an object rather than expressing an action, emotion, or quality such as size or color. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Leviticus 24:2. Its precise role there depends on the surrounding verse text, but its basic meaning remains a material description: something connected with or fashioned from olive wood.

This verb means “inject; cast in”—to put or throw something into another place or thing. It describes an action of placing something inside, whether by casting it in or inserting it. In the Greek Old Testament and related books, it occurs 73 times, so its exact force can vary with what is being placed and where. Its earliest recorded occurrence is in Genesis 31:34, and it continues through books including Exodus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Daniel.

This word means “eleven,” the whole number that comes after ten and before twelve. It is a number word used to state a count, quantity, or position. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 14 times, including descriptions of groups, measured items, and numbered days or years. Its basic meaning remains the same wherever it appears; the surrounding sentence determines what is being counted. This is a Greek LXX word and should be understood within that Greek Old Testament corpus.

This word means “liable” or “guilty”: it describes someone held responsible for a wrong and answerable for it. As an adjective, it characterizes a person who bears responsibility, rather than naming the wrongdoing itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 20 times, most often rendered “guilty,” with “liable” also appearing. Its use ranges across laws and accounts of wrongdoing, so the surrounding sentence identifies what person or offense is in view. The central idea is being responsible for an offense.

Propitiate means to seek favor or goodwill by making an appeal or offering intended to satisfy displeasure. It is a verb describing an action directed toward reconciliation or acceptance. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, this word occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 4:11. The available lexical meaning is “propitiate”; the surrounding verse would be needed to explain precisely what is being sought or offered in that passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “confession”: an open acknowledgment or declaration. It names the act of admitting or expressing something plainly, especially in relation to God or others. The word occurs 23 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this LXX corpus, so it is a recurring biblical expression rather than a rare technical term. Its precise emphasis can depend on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains confession—openly acknowledging what is true.

This Greek LXX verb means “come on up” or “come back.” It describes movement toward a place or a return to a previous place or situation. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings represented here, including uses in Genesis, Leviticus, Job, Proverbs, and 2 Maccabees. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is upward movement or returning.

In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), this word means “plotting against.” As an adjective, it describes someone or something acting against another through a scheme; as a noun, it can refer to a person characterized by that opposition. It occurs 13 times in the LXX corpus, including passages from Samuel, Kings, Habakkuk, and the Maccabean books. The surrounding verse determines who is being opposed and what the plotting involves.

This word means “call”: it describes summoning, naming, or inviting someone, depending on the sentence. As a verb in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it expresses an action directed toward a person or group. It occurs 21 times in this Greek corpus, across both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but the central idea remains calling someone or designating them by name.

This verb means “arrive also” or “come also up,” describing an additional arrival or movement upward. It presents someone as coming to a place or joining an arrival already mentioned. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 10:9. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is an added arrival or coming up.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “supervise” or “observe.” It describes paying attentive oversight to someone or something, with the purpose of watching carefully and exercising responsible care. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament, across six verses, including passages from Deuteronomy, Kings, Chronicles, Esther, and Proverbs. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is active, watchful oversight rather than merely seeing something casually.

This noun refers to profitmaking—the pursuit or practice of gaining financial benefit. It names an activity rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in Sirach 29:19. The word’s basic meaning is therefore focused and specific: making profit. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

Esrae, also rendered Ezrae, is a proper name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person or other named individual in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 1 Kings 4:12. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the identity and role of Esrae in that passage require the verse’s context.

This verb means being “in good health.” It describes a person’s healthy condition or well-being rather than an action performed on someone else. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 17:22, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense remains straightforward: to be healthy, sound, or physically well. [p03:word:lxx:L705571:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705571:occurrences]

This adjective describes someone who is easy of address—pleasant, approachable, and not difficult to speak with. It refers to a person whose manner welcomes conversation rather than making others hesitant or afraid. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament collection represented here, in Sirach 6:5. Its basic emphasis is on a person’s accessible manner in social interaction, though the surrounding verse would be needed to explain the precise force in that passage.

This adjective means “reverent,” describing someone or something marked by deep respect toward God or sacred things. It presents reverence as a recognizable quality rather than an action by itself. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, the word occurs 29 times, so it is used broadly across wisdom, prophetic, and other religious texts. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains respectful devotion expressed in a godly manner.

Ēlas, also rendered Ilas, is a proper name used to identify a particular person. It is not a general description or action word, but a personal designation. In the Greek Old Testament, this name appears twice: once in Genesis and once in 1 Chronicles. Without the surrounding verse text, the name alone does not establish further details about the person or the significance of either passage. Its plain function is to name someone. [p03:word:lxx:L705962:identity] [p03:word:lxx:L705962:occurrences]

This verb means to alarm or amaze someone. It describes an effect produced in a person, expressing strong surprise, astonishment, or sudden fear. The word can therefore point either to being alarmed or to being amazed, depending on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek Septuagint, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 6:8. Its basic sense remains the same: causing a person to react with intense surprise or alarm.

Thelamin is a proper name used to identify a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament. It does not describe an action, quality, or general idea, so its meaning is primarily its identifying function rather than a broader concept. Thelamin occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, at Numbers 13:22. The supplied lexical information gives the name itself but does not identify whether it refers to a person, place, or other kind of entity.

Theodotos, also rendered Theothotos, is a proper name rather than a general description or action. It identifies a particular person in the Greek Old Testament tradition preserved in the deuterocanonical books. The name occurs twice in this LXX corpus: once in 2 Maccabees 14:19 and once in 3 Maccabees 1:2. Without the surrounding verse text, its personal identity cannot be described further here, but its basic function is to name an individual.

This word means “break,” referring to a fracture, rupture, or state of being broken. It is a noun, so it names the break itself rather than describing the act of breaking. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nahum 2:11. The surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what kind of break is meant there, but the basic idea remains a separation, damage, or collapse from wholeness. Its precise force in that passage therefore depends on the context in which the noun appears.

Iassib, also rendered Iassiv, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament tradition. The name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Joshua 17:7, so its ordinary lexical function is simply to identify that individual. The available form does not provide a separate definition or explain the person’s role; those details belong to the surrounding passage rather than to the name itself.

Iemou, also rendered Iemu, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament and occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 7:2. Because the available wording gives only the name and no surrounding verse text, its personal identity and significance must be understood from that passage rather than from the name itself. The two forms, Iemou and Iemu, represent the same named individual in this lexical record.

Iesdri, also rendered Iezthri, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 25:11. The available lexical information preserves the name itself but does not provide an additional ordinary meaning or explanation of its name origin. Its precise identification and role in that passage depend on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This Greek LXX noun means “dwelling place,” referring to a place where someone lives or remains. It describes habitation rather than the person who inhabits it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah 30, appearing in Jeremiah 30:2 and Jeremiah 30:25. The surrounding passage is needed to explain the particular significance of the dwelling place in either verse, but the word itself points plainly to a residence or habitation.

Kataath is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears twice in this corpus, in Numbers 33:26 and Numbers 33:27. The name is presented as “Kataath,” with no further descriptive meaning attached to it in the available lexical information. Its precise reference is therefore determined by the surrounding passage, not by translating the name into another ordinary English term.

This LXX verb means “possess” or “give possession.” It describes taking possession of something or granting it as an inheritance or property. The word is used 56 times in the Greek Old Testament and related writings represented in this LXX corpus, especially in passages concerning land and its assignment. Its basic idea therefore concerns ownership being received or bestowed. The exact direction—whether someone possesses something or gives it into another’s possession—depends on how the verb functions in its sentence.

This verb means “sow thickly,” describing the act of scattering seed densely over ground. It presents sowing as abundant or closely distributed rather than merely placing a single seed. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, Job, and 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being sown and the surrounding sentence.

This word is a proper name, identified as “Kēdes; Kithes.” It functions as a specific name rather than a general description or action. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 11:63. The available information identifies the name and its location, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain exactly whom or what the name designates in that passage.

This noun means “clime,” referring to a particular region or area. It names a place or geographical part rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 47 times across 33 verses, so it is a recurring geographic term rather than a rare expression. Its use is especially concentrated in Exodus, though it also appears in Numbers, Psalms, 1 Kings, and Ezekiel. The precise sense in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording and the place being described.

This adverb means “in secret” or “secretly,” describing an action done privately or without being openly known. It tells how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Maccabees 10:79. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific action, but the word itself points to concealed or private action.

This verb means “make an uproar” or “spread alarm.” It describes creating loud disturbance or causing alarm to spread, rather than quietly communicating information. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 38:25, so its normal meaning is clear even though the immediate verse wording is not included here. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding context. The word functions as an action word describing a person or activity that produces commotion or alarm.

Lobeni is a proper name, rendered “Lobeni” and also “Loveni.” It functions as a personal or family name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs seven times, appearing in genealogical and family-list passages in Exodus, Numbers, and 1 Chronicles. The available wording identifies the name, but does not provide a separate definition or explain its origin. Its precise reference in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Lot is a proper name referring to the biblical person Lot. In the Greek Old Testament, the name appears chiefly in Genesis, where it is used for the man associated with Abram and his household. It occurs 36 times across 33 verses in this Greek Old Testament corpus, with 32 occurrences in Genesis. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is the identification of that individual; the surrounding passage is needed to explain what Lot is doing or experiencing in any particular verse.

This Greek LXX verb means “to be bald” and is also glossed “flaccid,” describing baldness or a limp condition. It occurs twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in Leviticus 13. As a verb, it expresses a condition or state rather than naming a person or object. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense concerns being bald or flaccid.

This adjective means “patient”: able to endure without giving way to anger or abandoning restraint. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it describes a quality of patient endurance. The word occurs 20 times in this LXX corpus, appearing especially in descriptions of God as patient and in statements about how people should respond. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This verb means “gnaw”: to bite or chew something persistently. It describes an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 30:4, so its ordinary meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not available here. The word should therefore be understood in its basic sense of repeated biting or chewing, while the precise force of the action depends on the sentence where it appears.

This verb means to make something smaller or to lessen it. It describes a reduction in size, extent, or degree rather than an increase. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 43:7. The surrounding verse is needed to identify precisely what is being reduced there, but the word itself expresses the action of diminishing or making less. It functions as an action word, describing what someone or something does.

This verb means “get by mining.” It describes obtaining something through mining rather than simply receiving or finding it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times: once in Deuteronomy and twice in Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains gaining what is needed through mining activity.

This word means “night-raven,” the name of a bird. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament to identify this creature rather than to describe an action or quality. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in passages from Leviticus, Deuteronomy, 1 Samuel, and Psalms. Its precise significance in any one passage comes from the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains the bird’s name. The clearest English rendering is “night-raven.”

This noun means “slugishness”—a state of being slow, inactive, or lacking readiness to act. It describes a quality rather than an action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 4:5. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but the word’s central idea is sluggishness: an absence of alertness, energy, or prompt movement.

This word means “administration”: the responsible management or ordering of affairs. As a noun, it refers to an arrangement of oversight rather than an action someone performs in a single moment. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Isaiah 22, so its use there is limited to two verses within this corpus. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular force in either passage, but its central idea remains organized responsibility or management.

This adjective means “visible”: something that can be seen or is perceptible to the eyes. It describes an observable thing rather than something hidden or unseen. In the Greek LXX, it occurs four times, all in Old Testament verses, including passages from 2 Samuel, 1 Chronicles, and Job. Its basic sense remains straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what visible thing is being described.

gl: put on/under oath; administer an oath
d: put on/under oath; administer an oath

e.t: This Greek LXX verb means to “put on/under oath” or “administer an oath.” It describes the act of binding someone by an oath, requiring a solemn pledge or compelling a sworn statement. The word is used 27 times in the Greek Old Testament, so it represents a recurring action rather than a rare technical expression. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on who administers the oath and what commitment or testimony is being required.

Ouriel, also rendered Uril, is a proper name used to identify a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Chronicles: three times in 1 Chronicles and once in 2 Chronicles. The available information establishes the name’s identity and usage, but does not provide a separate descriptive definition or explain the significance of the individuals who bear it. Its precise reference in any one passage must therefore be understood from that passage’s surrounding text.

This verb means “wrestle”: to engage another in physical struggle or grappling. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times in three verses, so its basic sense is focused and concrete rather than a broad label for every kind of conflict. It appears twice in Genesis 32 and once in Esther 1. The surrounding passage is needed to explain what the wrestling refers to in a particular verse, but the word itself describes the act of grappling or struggling bodily.

This verb means “press close; hold.” It describes the action of keeping something tightly against or near something else, or holding it firmly. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Kings 6:32. Because the word is a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central idea is firm pressure or close restraint.

A proverb is a concise saying that expresses wisdom or instruction in a memorable form. This Greek LXX noun refers to a proverb as a recognizable kind of teaching, rather than to a person, action, or place. It appears seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, especially in Proverbs and Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “helmet,” a protective covering worn on the head. It is a noun used for military or defensive equipment, including the headgear associated with warriors and armor. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 10 times: nine times in the Old Testament and once in the Deuterocanonical writings. Its central idea remains consistent—a helmet is something placed on the head to guard it in battle or danger.

This noun means “embracing,” referring to the act of taking hold of someone or something with the arms. It names an act rather than describing a person or command. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ecclesiastes 3:5. The word’s basic sense is therefore straightforward: an embrace or act of holding close. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This noun means “mistake in music” or “false note.” It names something incorrectly sounded or out of tune, using musical error as its defining image. In this Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs 48 times across the Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so it is not limited to one isolated passage. Its references include Leviticus, Joshua, Numbers, Ezra, and Sirach. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding wording.

This Greek LXX noun refers to the use of varied colours or to embroidery—the making of patterned or decorated work. It can describe ornamented material, skilled decorative work, or the process of adding coloured design, rather than a general statement about variety. The word occurs eight times in the Greek LXX corpus, including passages from Exodus, Judges, Ezekiel, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the object or activity being described.

This word describes something “conspicuous”—plainly visible, noticeable, or standing out so that it can be readily recognized. It may function as an adjective describing a person, thing, or condition, and its related noun use can refer to what is conspicuous. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in 2 Maccabees. The word’s basic sense remains focused on clear visibility or obvious prominence; the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being noticed.

This Greek LXX verb means being ready and willing to act. It describes a person who offers himself or herself freely, with preparedness rather than reluctance. The idea can apply to volunteering, responding, or taking part in a task. It occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, so its basic sense is consistent across several settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek Old Testament verb means to approach or go ahead—to move toward someone or something. It can describe coming near, proceeding forward, or taking the next step in an action. The word appears 101 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it serves as a normal action word across many passages rather than naming one special kind of approach. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on what or whom the subject approaches.

This word means “wing,” the body part associated with a bird’s flight. As a noun, it refers to a wing or wings in the Greek Old Testament, whether describing birds or wing-shaped features. It occurs 77 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, with frequent use in Ezekiel, Psalms, and the accounts of the temple. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Reu is a personal name identifying a person in the Old Testament’s Greek translation. It is not a common noun describing an object, action, or quality. This name occurs five times in the LXX corpus: four times in Genesis 11 and once in 1 Chronicles 1. The available lexical definition identifies the name simply as “Reu,” so its ordinary meaning here is the person’s name rather than a separate concept or description.

This word means “pomegranate,” the fruit known for its round shape and many seeds. It is a noun used for the fruit itself in the Greek Old Testament. The word appears 14 times across 12 verses in that corpus, including passages mentioning pomegranates among the produce of the land and in ornamental designs. Its ordinary meaning remains the same whether it refers to food, agricultural abundance, or decorative imagery.

Sapphire is the name of a precious gemstone. In the Greek Old Testament, this noun refers to sapphire as a valuable stone used in descriptions of costly materials, treasured objects, and splendid settings. The word occurs 12 times across 12 verses, including passages in Exodus, Job, Isaiah, and other books. Its meaning remains focused on the gemstone itself rather than on an abstract quality or action. The surrounding verse determines what the sapphire contributes to each description.

“Sennaar” is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament, functioning as a specific name rather than a general description. The word occurs five times in the LXX, all in Genesis, from Genesis 10:10 through Genesis 14:9. Its meaning is therefore primarily its identified name, and the surrounding verse is needed to explain what is being named in any particular occurrence.

Soma is a proper name, functioning as the name of a specific person or place in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once, in Joshua 15:52, and is rendered “Soma.” Because the verse text and surrounding context are not available here, the name’s precise referent cannot be identified from this word alone. Its lexical meaning is therefore simply the name “Soma,” rather than a descriptive word, action, or quality.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “row”: a set of things arranged beside or after one another in an orderly line. It is used for organized rows of stones or other items, especially in descriptions of the priestly garments and the tabernacle furnishings. The word occurs 21 times in the Greek Old Testament, in 14 verses, with uses found in Exodus and 1 Kings. Its basic idea is arrangement in a line or series, while the surrounding passage identifies what has been placed in that row.

This Greek Old Testament adjective means “all together” or “all at once.” It describes people, things, or actions viewed collectively, emphasizing that the whole group is included or that something happens in a single combined moment. The word appears 15 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Job, Psalms, Ezekiel, Isaiah, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on what group or action the surrounding sentence presents.

This Greek LXX noun means “chance; casualty.” It refers to an occurrence or outcome viewed as happening by chance, and it can also name a casualty or misfortune. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, in four verses, so it is an uncommon word rather than a broad, frequently repeated term. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Greek LXX verb means to bear something to completion or maturity. It describes bringing a process, result, or living thing toward its fully developed end, rather than leaving it unfinished. As a verb, it expresses an action or process of reaching maturity. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees, so its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage. Its central idea remains clear: bringing forth something fully developed or completed.

d: terebinth tree; fruit from terebinth tree

e.t: This noun refers to a terebinth tree or to fruit from such a tree. It identifies a particular kind of tree rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs twice, once in Joshua and once in Sirach. The surrounding verse determines whether the reference is to the tree itself or its fruit, but the basic meaning remains connected with the terebinth plant.

This noun refers to the end or boundary of something—the point where it finishes or reaches its limit. It can describe a terminating point, an outer limit, or the final extent of a thing. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in 1 Kings and once in Wisdom. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on a physical boundary or an ending, but the central idea remains a limit or conclusion.

This LXX conjunction and particle means “for then actually.” It links a statement with what follows, giving the words a force of explanation, conclusion, or emphasis. In ordinary English, it can help introduce something presented as the real or resulting point. It occurs 11 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books represented here, including Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek LXX verb means “overstep”: to go beyond a proper limit or boundary. It describes crossing what should not be crossed, whether a physical boundary or an established limit. The word occurs 17 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, so its basic sense is used in more than one setting. Its exact force in any verse depends on what boundary or limit the surrounding passage identifies.

This Greek LXX verb means “cause to collapse”: it describes bringing someone or something down so that it falls or loses its ability to stand. As a verb, it expresses an action performed by one agent upon another person or thing, rather than merely describing a state of weakness. It occurs once in the Greek text represented here, in Sirach 12:17. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

Pharai is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It is rendered in the gloss as “Pharai” and “Fare.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Samuel 23:35. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further; its basic meaning is the personal designation Pharai.

This Greek LXX verb means to express something in words or to claim or state something. It describes the act of saying what one thinks, knows, or declares, rather than naming a person or object. The word occurs 72 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so it can describe ordinary speech as well as formal statements. Its precise force in any verse depends on what is being expressed or claimed there.

This verb means “burn” or “burn up,” describing something consumed or affected by fire. In the Greek Old Testament, it can describe literal burning and imagery of intense fire. The word occurs 10 times across the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so its central idea remains consistent while the surrounding passage determines whether the fire is physical or figurative. It appears in passages from Exodus, Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, and Jeremiah, among others.

This Greek LXX noun refers to a groat, meaning a hulled kernel of grain prepared for use as food or an offering. It names the kernel after its outer covering has been removed, rather than describing a person or an action. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, all in Leviticus, where its use belongs to instructions concerning grain offerings and the presentation of early produce. Its precise significance in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning is a prepared, hulled grain kernel.

This noun means “shoulder” or “side.” It can refer to the shoulder area of the body, or to a side or lateral part of something. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 13 times across 9 verses, including descriptions involving people and constructed objects. The surrounding context determines whether “shoulder” or “side” best expresses the word in a particular passage. Its basic idea remains a physical side or shoulder rather than an abstract quality or action.

This Greek LXX word means “as such; that.” It functions as a conjunction, adverb, or particle, helping connect parts of a sentence and express how one statement relates to another. It is a commonly used connective word in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, occurring 171 times across 162 verses. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding words, but its basic role is to link or qualify a statement rather than name a person, object, or action.
